newsitem.title: USA: Rescuers search for more victims of Texas twisters.
newsitem.headline: Rescuers search for more victims of Texas twisters.

text.p: Rescue workers on Wednesday picked through the splintered remains of a rural neighborhood searching for victims of a powerful tornado that killed at least 27 people and left dozens homeless.
The death toll was expected to rise, with another 23 people reported missing in Jarrell, Texas, where a neighborhood was leveled by the twister, police said.
"We certainly do hope we find some survivors," Williamson County Sheriff Ed Richards said. "It looks like a war zone out there. It's just completely flattened."

At least six tornadoes ripped through the heart of Texas during spring storms on Tuesday that also brought torrential rains and baseball-sized hail. At least two people died in Austin, including a man whose house was struck by a tornado and a girl who drowned in a rain-swollen creek, police said.
In nearby Cedar Park, rescue workers and search dogs combed a grocery store for several people missing after the building's roof collapsed during the storm, Texas police spokesman Mike Cox said.

"There's still believed to be four to five missing at that Albertson's store in Cedar Park," Cox said. A worker was found in critical condition on Tuesday and five unclaimed cars in the parking lot may belong to victims, police said.

In San Antonio, 106 mph (170 kph) winds were clocked at Kelly Air Force Base as the storm roared through the area. About 100,000 people were temporarily without power overnight and 27 residents were left homeless when the roof was ripped off their building in an apartment complex, police said.

Rescue workers in Jarrell slogged through knee-deep mud looking for victims in the demolished subdivision while survivors waited for news of friends and families still missing in the twisted wreckage.
As dawn broke in this small town about 40 miles (62 km) north of Austin, the storm's fury was marked by a 1 mile (1.6 km) long, quarter-mile wide swath cut through the subdivision.

"I've never seen anything in my entire law enforcement career this massive and this destructive. It's totally wiped clean ... total, massive destruction," Williamson County Constable Gary Griffin said.
For the people of Jarrell, population 650, the tornado brought back memories of another twister that hit almost exactly eight years ago. But only one person died then.
Tuesday's tornado was a force of nature they hoped never to witness again.
"This one sounded like a bear growling, low tones, an evil sound," said 17-year-old Danny Williams, who took refuge with his father when the tornado passed near their home.
Along with the 27 people that police said were confirmed dead, rescue workers found dozens of dead cattle, dogs, horses and even an ostrich.
"I kept hearing gunshots going off and I couldn't figure out what it was. I realized later they were shooting animals who had been hurt," Deputy Constable Priscilla Smith said.

Police said as many as 50 houses and mobile homes were destroyed when the tornado struck Jarrell, which sits in in rolling cattle country at the eastern edge of the Texas Hill Country. In all, about 200 buildings were damaged or destroyed across a four-county area by the six twisters.

Jimmy Wingo of the Morgan's Point Volunteer Fire Department on nearby Lake Belton said 310 boats were damaged by a tornado. "They're scattered from one end of the lake to the other. From what I've seen, it's mass chaos," he said.
The dead were placed in a makeshift morgue in the city's small fire department and the bodies of 26 victims were transported to the Travis County medical examiner's facility.
